grammar.title: Εἰ … ἐάν … ἄν
grammar.rule: εἰ … ἴδοιμι, ὠργιζόμην · εἰ … εἴη, ἂν … ἐκβάλλοι · εἰ … ᾔδειν, ἂν … ἦλθον

tables.caption: Εἰ … ἐάν … ἄν
rows: εἰ οὗτος τὸν λίθον μετεκίνησεν, ἐγὼ οὐκ ἐκέλευσα (s024)
if this man moved the stone, I did not order it: μετεκίνησεν = he moved; ἐκέλευσα = I ordered
ἐὰν ὁ Δαμάρετος τὰ δῶρα δέξηται, φίλος ἡμῖν ἔσται (s007)
if Damaretus accepts the gifts, he will be our friend: δέξηται = he accepts; ἔσται = he will be
εἰ δὲ κινήσεις, ἐκβαλῶ σε ἐκ τῆς οἰκίας (s044) · εἰ δὲ τὰ πρόβατα αὐτοῦ τοῦ ἔαρος ἐκεῖ ἔσται, ὁ Σωσίας αὐτὰ πάλιν ἐκβαλεῖ (s061)

but if you move it, I will throw you out of the house: κινήσεις = you will move; ἐκβαλῶ = I will throw out; if his sheep are there in spring, Sosias will drive them out again: ἔσται = they will be (neuter plural subject); ἐκβαλεῖ = he will drive out
εἰ οὖν τοῦ χειμῶνος κοινὴ εἴη ἡ νομή, οὐδεὶς ἂν τὰ πρόβατα ἐκβάλλοι (s058)
if the pasture were to be shared in winter, nobody would drive out the sheep: εἴη = it were to be; ἐκβάλλοι = would drive out
φθονῶ σοι, ἐὰν τοὺς σοὺς ἵππους ἐν τῷ κλήρῳ τοῦ πατρὸς ἴδω (s038)
I envy you whenever I see your horses on my father’s plot: φθονῶ = I envy; ἴδω = I see
εἴ ποτε χειμὼν χαλεπὸς εἴη, οἱ ἡμέτεροι ποιμένες τὰ πρόβατα ἐκεῖ ἔνεμον (s057)
whenever a winter was hard, our shepherds used to pasture the sheep there: εἴη = was; ἔνεμον = they used to pasture
εἰ δὲ ᾔδειν, πρῶτον ἂν πρὸς σὲ ἦλθον (s035)
but if I had known, I would have come to you first: ᾔδειν = I had known; ἦλθον = I would have come
εἰ δὲ Λάκων ἦσθα, οὐκ ἂν οὕτω πρᾶος ἦσθα (s076)
but if you were a Spartan, you would not be so gentle: first ἦσθα = you were; second ἦσθα with ἄν = you would be

grammar.note_en:
Read the two verbs together. A protasis is the if-clause; an apodosis is the main clause saying what follows. The if-clause alone does not always identify the condition. In this chapter Damaretus remembers a repeated experience, and Xenophon proposes an arrangement. Both use εἰ with an optative. The main verb tells you which world you are in.

Damaretus says «Εἴ ποτε χειμὼν χαλεπὸς εἴη, οἱ ἡμέτεροι ποιμένες τὰ πρόβατα ἐκεῖ ἔνεμον» (s057): “Whenever a winter was hard, our shepherds used to pasture the sheep there.” Εἴη is the present optative of εἰμί, but it does not by itself mean “would be.” Here ἔνεμον is an imperfect indicative: the shepherds actually did this, repeatedly, in the past. There is no ἄν. The optative presents the recurring circumstance within that past pattern. Likewise «Καὶ γὰρ εἴ ποτε τὸν λίθον ἐκεῖνον ἴδοιμι, ὠργιζόμην» (s026), “And indeed, whenever I saw that stone, I used to get angry”: ἴδοιμι is aorist optative, ὠργιζόμην imperfect indicative. Seeing is viewed as an occasion; the anger was the recurring response. Neither optative makes the experience unreal.

Now Xenophon: «Εἰ οὖν τοῦ χειμῶνος κοινὴ εἴη ἡ νομή, οὐδεὶς ἂν τὰ πρόβατα ἐκβάλλοι» (s058), “If, then, the pasture were to be shared in winter, nobody would drive out the sheep.” The same εἴη now belongs to a future less-vivid condition, an imagined proposal rather than a past habit. The main clause has ἐκβάλλοι, another optative, with ἄν: “would drive out.” Nothing in the label “less vivid” means that the speaker thinks the arrangement unlikely. He is offering it for consideration, not predicting it as settled.

Compare the open future promise «Ἐὰν τοῦτο γένηται, πάλιν σοι τυρὸν οἴσω» (s082), “If that happens, I will bring you cheese again.” Γένηται is aorist subjunctive after ἐάν; οἴσω is future indicative. The future most-vivid warning «Εἰ δὲ κινήσεις, ἐκβαλῶ σε ἐκ τῆς οἰκίας» (s044), “But if you move it, I will throw you out of the house,” uses future indicative in both halves. Neither main clause adds ἄν.

Finally «εἰ δὲ ᾔδειν, πρῶτον ἂν πρὸς σὲ ἦλθον» (s035), “But if I had known, I would have come to you first,” has past indicatives and main-clause ἄν. This is contrary to fact: Xenophon did not know. An imperfect can instead describe an unreal present, as ἦσθα “you were” does at s076. So check both moods, check where ἄν stands, then use context for time. Do not translate every optative with “would,” or every past indicative as past time.

Gryllus now uses the same future/future pair at s061: «Εἰ δὲ τὰ πρόβατα αὐτοῦ τοῦ ἔαρος ἐκεῖ ἔσται … ὁ Σωσίας αὐτὰ πάλιν ἐκβαλεῖ», “But if his sheep are there in spring, Sosias will drive them out again.” Both ἔσται and ἐκβαλεῖ are future indicative; the singular ἔσται agrees with the neuter plural τὰ πρόβατα.

parergon.title: ἄν
parergon.body_en: In the ordinary conditions here, separate ἄν belongs in the main clause: optative + ἄν means “would”; past indicative + ἄν marks the unreal result. Ordinary εἰ-clauses do not take it. Ἐάν already combines εἰ and ἄν and takes the subjunctive; do not add another ἄν to its future or present-indicative main clause. The authentic s126 is an explicitly receptive exception: Xenophon puts a potential optative with ἄν inside the εἰ-clause. Recognise that as “if he should not obtain …,” not as a model for making conditions. No exercise asks you to produce it.

families.spelling_note: Canonical ἀπο- appears as ἀπ- before the vowel of ἀλλάττω: ἀπο- → ἀπ-αλλάττομαι (s073). Canonical δια- loses its final vowel before the root: δια- → δι-αλλάττω; augment lengthens the root’s initial α, giving δι-ηλλάγημεν (s069), aorist passive, “we were reconciled.” Both meanings are non-compositional: neither is merely a spatial sum of prefix and “change.” Damaretus gets free of a dangerous affair; the two neighbours become reconciled. The simple verb at s033 is locally glossed only, not counted as a new course lexeme.
